en: Her rib bones coming apart,
Tears pouring from her eyes,
Unable to stay still, wailing and sobbing,
Unable to restrain her tears,
Her poor heart torn apart,
When she heard news of her only son,
Helpless, sobbing,
To God whose decree is mighty,
She prayed and cried aloud.
To reach Semetey,
For the orphan granted in her last extremity,
To offer herself as a sacrifice,
Despairing of all the world,
Your royal mother Kanykey
Ran in great haste.
To see Semetey,
If his illness was real,
To die before her destined death.
To run and reach Semetey,
Her two eyes becoming four,
For the orphan left by her companion,
If his illness was true,
To offer herself as a sacrifice,
For six calves and four yearling horses,
The bright knife she had bought,
To draw it from its sheath,
To offer this damned life
As a sacrifice.
Running breathlessly over the pass,
Hurrying along on foot,
The one God had granted
What she had asked for.
Crossing one mountain pass after another,
Pale and bewildered,
The hilt slipping from her hand,
The covering slipping from her heart,
The red blood draining from her face,
Her senses fled, her strength was gone.
Your dear mother Kanykey
Had come directly before
Her own child.
When he saw his mother,
The orphan could not restrain his excitement,
There he beheld his mother.
Before him was his refuge;
He beheld her brow.
The one he would approach in worship,
His beloved object of devotion, he beheld.
The one God had truly
Granted what he had asked.
Plainly recognizing his mother,
The heroic orphan Manas left behind
Had truly seen her!
He stretched out his hand and spoke:
“My shelter, my mother,” he said.
“The dark ridge stretching before me—
You are my net to catch the wild game,
My mother who has sheltered me—
I thought you my sister, but you are my mother!
You are my Night of Power when I wish,
You are my one and only before me.
When my ocean-like father died,
My countless treasures and riches
You came away scattering.
Wandering to your birth family, Mother,
You came away in flight.
With all reason gone from your heart,
You came away in haste.
Is there cause for a khan's
Only child to go in flight?
Alas, Mother, where are our people?
Is there cause for a lord's
Only child to wander abroad?
My valiant mother, where are our people?
When will we reach our people?
Wandering to Bukhara for support,
You came and lodged with Khan Temir;
You came and settled with your birth family.
You made them call me Manas's wandering son,
You gave me a bad name.
Is there cause to wander
In Khan Temir's city?
My ocean-like mother, where are our people?
Is there cause to flee and lodge
In Khan Ismayyl's city?
Where are the honored Kyrgyz people?
Alas, my mother Kanykey,
When will we reach our people?
Akolpok, left by my father,
The costly coat with its golden collar,
Mother, you came without wearing it.
Such is your womanly folly:
Fleeing and wandering to Bukhara,
You came without understanding.
My father's own brother,
My uncle Abyke,
You came without marrying him.
You came and settled in Bukhara;
‘This orphan came here wandering,’ they say—
You have given us a bad name!”
So Semetey said,
And when he had spoken,
When he had uttered
Those very grievous, painful words:
“Oh, my dear little brother,
May that foul mouth fill with blood!
What creature says such things?
Oh, little brother, stop!” she said.
The impetuous woman sprang up.
Semetey stretched out
His hand toward his mother.
In her haste, Kanykey
Gave the boy her hand.
Without a slip in her words,
Calling him little brother, deceiving him greatly,
Kanykey answered him.
Now the boy heard her false words;
Semetey, left by the hero,
Now burned with rage!
The khan's only child
Seized her hand;
The ill-fated orphan slave
Clutched it hard.
Unable to endure his grip,
Burning with pain and shrieking,
Helpless and in agony,
She burst out sobbing:
“Let go of my hand, orphan!
My foal, do not dig my pit!
My foal, do not keep stirring up
My far-off misery.
Now I shall sing my song;
Alas, orphan, let go!
Now I shall tell my truth.
When your father Manas died,
You, the male child left behind, were young;
All the scoundrels were enemies.
When they plundered my possessions,
When the dogs wrought havoc,
The drop flowing from Alai,
Has not yet left my fat rump—
My foal, the slave Abyke's whip.
I have more words to tell:
I, your bereaved, hapless mother,
Where the six scoundrels struck,
Still bear the mark upon my breast.
Will God take me if I lament?
Back then, when I carried you,
Fleeing in grief and wandering,
When I wandered away in winter,
Through the great Syr-Darya's waters,
When I trudged across forty-two times,
God confounding my thoughts,
Clasping the child to my breast,
My widowhood made plain,
I put my mother on my shoulders,
That poor unfortunate woman.
Will God take me if I lament?
Will the ice that formed on my calves
Ever leave my very bones?
My foal, Abyke and Kobosh, two scoundrels,
From these I suffered humiliation.
Chyybyt and Kochkor, four scoundrels,
From those I suffered arrogance.
Adybay and Kolbay, six scoundrels,
I truly suffered humiliation, my son.
Back then, I, your mother Kanykey,
Could not cross Kuyuk Pass,
Could not walk, grieving and wandering,
Could not cross Jorgo Pass,
Poor soul, could not walk, grieving and weeping.
My overshoes wore out; I was in felt stockings.
Though I grieved, poor soul, I did not die.
My boots were gone; I was in felt stockings.
If the angel of death does not come,
It is hard for this soul to die!
I could not ford along the Syr-Darya;
I lost my composure, wretched soul,
Weeping bitterly, unable to pass,
Unable to reach a waist-deep place,
The Syr-Darya's waters are a mighty river;
Saying, ‘I shall trudge across forty-two times,’
Unable to ford that river,
Water penetrating to my marrow,
My very bones aching and throbbing,
I sobbed, finding no way out.
There was no hollow where I could lie,
No food to put in my mouth;
My mother, ninety-five, wept and shrieked.
My senses fled, my strength was gone;
Though I hurried, I could not cross.
When I was helpless,
My uncle Bakay, bringing good fortune,
His towering presence like a host of troops,
My aged lord Bakay—
My saint left by your father Manas,
Who had planted your sultan father Manas
And made him into a garden,
Who had built him into a house,
Who had led him and made him a hero,
Made him a lion before all the world,
Opened a path where none led through,
Freed an army when it was hemmed in,
Wearing a cap of gray lynx,
Wielding a mottled blue shield,
Six months of hardship
He pondered even now—
Who found words in sudden danger,
Found sight in darkness,
The lion Bakay, left by your father Manas,
That dear lion had understood.
Wearing out his horse, scouting the road,
Crying out, ‘Kanykey!’
Bringing a letter for my father, Khan Temir,
Bringing two skins of milk,
Bringing two swift horses,
He somehow got us across the water,
Kindled my extinguished fire,
Revived my dead soul.
With his thoughts still more disturbed,
Nuzzling your eyes all the more,
Not letting go of the child,
‘When a woman's husband dies,
Her birth family becomes dear,’ he said.
Taking my hand and embracing me,
Alas, my uncle Bakay,
Entrusting you, left by the lord,
Told me, ‘Flee to Bukhara,’
And I came wandering to Bukhara.
Khan Bakay had given the command;
My uncle, who was like a prophet,
I, a widow, obeyed,
And gave you to my kinsman Ismayyl!
The khan of Alty-Shaar, Kokand,
Used to impose heavy tribute.
Six thousand silver ingots, a thousand otter skins,
He used to take in tribute.
Unable to endure the tribute,
That Sart would now and then
Commit hostile acts.
‘The khan of Alty-Shaar, Kokand,
Will be a bitter enemy,’ I thought.
‘He will seize the orphan,
Before he comes of age,
And put him to death,’ I thought.
Cutting his ritual rod,
Performing the rite for him,
Making him step over a dog's bowl,
I gave him to Ismayyl.
‘They will destroy me altogether,’ I thought;
There are many enemies to fight.
‘Before you grow to maturity,
They will cut off your head,’ I thought.
I had an amulet hung about your neck,
Had my father Khan Temir raise you.
